newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian farmers have little trust in candidates.
newsitem.headline: Romanian farmers have little trust in candidates.

text.p: A pig and five geese rooted in the muddy yard of Constatin Danciu, oblivious to election posters plastered on electricity poles in this disheveled Romanian village.
The 1,500 residents of Ciorogirla, 16 km (10 miles) west of Bucharest, appeared equally perplexed by Sunday's presidential and parliamentary polls.
Most were more concerned with surviving on meagre incomes and how to scratch together enough money for Christmas.
"Life is tough here," said Danciu, 57. "It was a bad year for crops and my family has to survive on my small pension. What else can I say?"
Danciu said he intended to vote for President Ion Iliescu, who has been in power in Romania since the 1989 revolution which ousted dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.

Iliescu draws much of his support from rural areas and with three days left, he holds a small lead in opinion surveys. The president will almost certainly face a run-off against one of his two main rivals.
But Danciu had no intention of backing the president's Party of Social Democracy (PDSR), which trails in second place in polls for the parliamentary election.
"I doubt any of these PDSR guys can do anything for us," Danciu said, gesturing at a half dozen posters promoting the ruling party's candidates for both houses of parliament.
Ciorogirla's role supplying vegetables to Bucharest makes it relatively well off by the standards of Romania's countryside, where horse-drawn carts remain the main means of transport.
By Christmas, Danciu's pig will be fat enough to augment supplies of bacon and sausage. In the meantime, he relies on a pension of 200,000 lei ($50) a month to feed a family of four.
"All these politicians did was drive through the village and leave behind promises, leaflets and coloured balloons. They are no help," Danciu said.
His neighbour, Gheorghe Ciobanu, complained farmers faced huge costs to bring in the harvest after repeated fuel and equipment price increases.
"You might pay over 100,000 lei ($25) to have a hectare ploughed and sown," he said. "That's more than what the crop would fetch at the market."
Ciorogirla, which means "Crow Creek" in Romanian, has few amenities.

Two bars serve the local male population and a room in a private house has been converted into a small shop selling chocolate, liquor and a few other goods. A white brick Orthodox church is well tended, as is a school.
All parties in the election have promised to develop the countryside, offering farmers cheap loans to buy equipment and pay for harvesting work.

Romania has been slow to complete an ambitious 1991 land redistribution, under which 4.3 million farmers are entitled to recover small plots from state holdings created when communists nationalised land in the 1950s.

"The law is bad," Vlad Vlad (correct) of Propact, a union of private land owners which claims more than a million members, told Reuters in Bucharest. He blamed red tape and corruption for slow progress in the farming sector.
High start-up costs and interest rates made purchase of farming equipment a "remote dream" for many, he said. "Let's hope Sunday's elections will change things into better."
